extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, researchers in mathematical aesthetics, and people designing evaluation rubrics or automated metrics for mathematical work
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and applying a rubric (or quantitative metric) to evaluate the aesthetic quality of mathematical objects—especially proofs—using empirically grounded, cross-cultural comparative judgments. Emphasizes aggregation across raters and methodological choices that yield a continuous beauty parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematician consensus as a real signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Can rely on mathematician consensus as a real signal — aesthetic judgments about mathematical beauty are not purely private or idiosyncratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community agreement as evidence of an underlying beauty parameter rather than treating beauty as entirely subjective; consensus was robust within groups and across British and Chinese mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate across multiple raters
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric should aggregate responses from multiple mathematicians to extract the shared beauty parameter for a piece of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect many judgments rather than relying on single raters; aggregation reduces noise and captures the shared ranking evident in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer pairwise comparative judgments over Likert ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pairwise comparisons ('which of these two proofs is more beautiful?') rather than direct 1–10 ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative-judgment avoids limitations of Likert scales, yields finer discrimination, and produces data appropriate for models that infer a continuous latent beauty parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probabilistic ranking models (Bradley–Terry / Thurstonian) to extract beauty parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate pairwise comparison data with models (e.g., Bradley–Terry or Thurstonian) to infer a single continuous beauty parameter per item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These models convert pairwise wins/losses into an interval-scale parameter suitable for ranking and further analysis; recommended as part of any empirical rubric implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rank judgments from adjective labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate robust rank-based judgments (which proofs are more beautiful) from less-robust adjective assignments (e.g., 'elegant' vs 'beautiful' vs 'deep').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rubrics to emphasize ranking/relative scoring rather than relying on subjective adjective choice, which may be shifted by social pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability across cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful item should be placed high on the inferred parameter consistently across cultures (evidence from British and Chinese samples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When validating a rubric, check cross-cultural stability; lack of stability across cultures calls for further examination of item selection or cultural influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability across expertise levels
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric should yield similar high placement for the same items across expertise levels (undergraduates and research-active mathematicians both ranked items similarly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect experts to show lower variance (less noise); include both novices and experts when testing rubric generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diverse panel composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a diverse panel of mathematicians (culturally and by expertise) to infer a robust beauty ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity in the judging panel helps ensure the inferred parameter reflects shared features rather than group-specific preferences; the study used British mathematicians, Chinese mathematicians, and British undergraduates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically calibrate rubric on benchmark set
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibrate and validate the rubric by collecting comparative judgments on a curated benchmark of mathematical items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a benchmark set of well-chosen proofs/theorems/formulae and use it to map features to the inferred beauty parameter; this enables empirical grounding for auto-metric development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness implies objectively detectable features
rubrics_metrics.description: Because agreement is robust, the features underlying beauty should be objectively detectable and thus measurable by future automated rubrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design feature detectors (compactness, insight density, etc.) that correlate with the empirically derived beauty parameter; use regression or predictive modelling against the benchmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement across mathematical object types
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreement structure holds across proofs, theorems, and formulae — not just one object type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the rubric to multiple mathematical object types and verify consistent rankings; do not assume a rubric validated only on proofs will transfer without testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness / economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A component of mathematical beauty: the proof expresses ideas with economy—compact presentation relative to content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measures of length vs conceptual content, concision, and minimality when operationalizing this component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising compression
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful proof achieves surprising compression: it conveys deep results with unexpectedly little machinery or exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the ratio of conceptual depth to explicit apparatus; detect instances where a short argument yields a big conceptual payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty can arise when a proof unifies concepts across different domains or previously separate areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score unificatory breadth (links between fields) or the use of ideas from one domain to resolve problems in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense that the result and its derivation feel necessary or natural contributes to beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize inevitability via measures of logical naturalness, canonical steps, or the degree to which the proof seems forced rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generativity
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful item opens up further questions or avenues of work; it is generative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the proof suggests extensions, corollaries, or new directions; include citation/derivative-work proxies when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insight density
rubrics_metrics.description: High ratio of conceptual content (insight) to textual or technical length — many ideas packed tightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure conceptual moves per unit length, or count key novel ideas versus exposition; insight density should correlate positively with inferred beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curation/generalizability caveat (classical proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used curated, largely classical beautiful proofs; agreement may be lower for uncurated or frontier research items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the rubric to research frontiers, validate separately; do not assume the same level of consensus as found on classical benchmark items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited cultural sampling caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-cultural evidence in the study is limited to British and Chinese mathematicians; other cultures remain untested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend cross-cultural validation before generalizing beyond the sampled populations (e.g., Russian, Indian, African mathematicians).
